newsitem.title: USA: Ill. lawmakers open hearings on Tollway spending.
newsitem.headline: Ill. lawmakers open hearings on Tollway spending.

text.p: Illinois lawmakers opened hearings Wednesday into Illinois State Toll Highway Authority spending practices with veiled references to past corruption and charges of political grandstanding.

Toll Authority Chairman Julian D'Esposito conceded that the agency could have better relations with lawmakers, but he also testified that he expects the Illinois Supreme Court to vindicate its budget practices.

Cook County Judge Stephen Schiller in May overturned the Toll Authority's budget practices and gave the agency until December 15 to receive budget approval from the General Assembly or be enjoined from all expenditures except for debt service.

State Rep. Jeffrey Schoenberg, D-Evanston, called the hearing Wednesday to begin addressing Schiller's decision, which the Toll Authority and bond trustee for nearly $1 billion of its outstanding debt have appealed.
Schiller's decision would dramatically change the Toll Authority's business methods, if upheld, and clearly apply to expenditures by many other state entities, D'Esposito said.
Those changes could result in ratings downgrades or a refunding of the outstanding debt at a higher rate, D'Esposito said.

George Pitt, a Katten, Muchin & Zavis bond attorney, told lawmakers subjecting the budget to appropriation could result in more expensive credit. While it could be rehabilitated if it were downgraded, the process would be very complicated, Pitt said.

Even before hearing testimony from the scheduled witnesses, representatives alternately suggested legislative oversight of the Toll Authority would have complex and possibly negative implications for the state's bond rating or no fiscal impact at all.
Schoenberg, chairman of one of the two House appropriations committees convening the hearing and a Tollway critic, said it would be prudent to begin addressing the ruling.
Rep. Robert Biggins, R-Elmhurst, contended, however, that the hearing was "an exercise in futility" sparked by "mean-spiritedness."

Rep. Cal Skinner, R-Crystal Lake, suggested that some gasoline tax revenues now expended by the state transportation department on roads in other areas could be captured for use in Chicago metropolitan area.
Skinner, whose district borders the north suburban Chicago area, called D'Esposito an improvement over past Toll Authority leaders.
After one witness noted that more than a dozen lawmakers serve as Toll Authority board appointees, another lawmaker noted that former state Rep. Joseph Kotlarz had served in that capacity.
Kotlarz was convicted in April on state charges of conspiring to take Toll Authority funds through a public land sale.
